standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: PARENT LAYER: age-by-age RSE guidance mapped to your child's journey (bodies, consent, puberty, relationships, sexuality, online); many small talks; facts + your values (UNESCO 4.2, 6.3, 7.1, 2.1). New v2 build, the keystone of the Parent Layer and the hinge of the generational loop: a parent guided here becomes the trusted adult the kids' journey always assumed. The core reframe: it isn't one dreaded 'talk', it's many small, age-right conversations, and you can do them. Six modes: how to talk (start early, stay calm, answer 'I don't know' honestly, be the askable open door), the early years (correct body-part names, which protect against abuse and aid disclosure, body safety and consent basics, no body secrets, where-babies-come-from simply, consent in greetings), the middle years (prepare for puberty before it starts, periods and wet dreams for all children, online basics and reporting scary content), the teen talks (consent, online and porn-literacy against the manosphere, respect in relationships, staying askable through the eye-rolls), facts and your values (give honest facts AND share your values rather than choosing between them, because silence cedes the field to peers and the algorithm), tools and help (age-by-age guides, ready scripts, the open-door habit, and routing any child-safety concern to Be the Safe Adult g69). Protective and evidence-based throughout: correct names and talking make children safer, not more at risk, and age-appropriate, accurate, non-explicit guidance is expert-reviewed; it respects family values while keeping facts honest and never shames a parent for not knowing. Builds on (and mirrors) the kids' journey from My Body, My Rules (g02); around it sit the positive-parenting pillars (g65-g69). India: these conversations are too often never had, and silence and 'log kya kahenge' leave the internet and the manosphere to teach instead, so the node gently breaks the cycle with culturally-aware scripts, mindful of grandparents and joint families.

evidenceBase: Guiding a child's relationships-and-sexuality learning is many small, age-appropriate conversations over years rather than one dreaded 'talk', and the evidence is reassuring: honest, age-appropriate education is associated with later, not earlier, onset of sexual activity and with safer choices, so talking protects children rather than encouraging them, and the common fear that it 'gives ideas' is misinformation. The parent's job is to stay calm, answer at the child's level, say 'I don't know, let's find out together' when needed, and above all stay the askable, open door so the child keeps coming to them rather than the internet (UNESCO comprehensive sexuality education; WHO CSE evidence)

Early body-safety teaching is protective, not a loss of innocence: teaching young children the correct anatomical names for their body parts is a recognised safeguard, children who know them are more likely to be left alone by abusers and, if something does happen, to disclose clearly and be understood, while 'no body secrets', safe-versus-unsafe touch, and letting a child choose how to greet people teach consent and bodily autonomy from age four. As children approach puberty they should be prepared before the changes begin (ideally by around nine) so periods, wet dreams and body changes never come as a frightening shock, with all children learning about everyone's puberty to build empathy and end shame, alongside simple online-safety basics (child-sexual-abuse-prevention research; UNESCO/WHO age-appropriate guidance)

Through the teen years the door matters more, not less, and honest facts and family values belong together rather than in opposition: teens still want a trusted adult, online content and the manosphere often distort sex, bodies and respect, and a parent's honest, non-judgemental voice on consent, porn-literacy and respectful relationships is the antidote, with teaching consent being protective rather than 'giving ideas'. Parents do not have to choose between accurate facts and their own values, children can hold the facts to stay safe and the values to guide them, and withholding facts makes children more vulnerable while silence simply cedes the field to peers and the algorithm; the guidance is age-appropriate, accurate, non-explicit and expert-reviewed, never shames a parent for not knowing, and routes any child-safety concern to safeguarding support (Be the Safe Adult g69) (UNESCO ITGSE; comprehensive-sexuality-education and porn-literacy research; child-safeguarding practice)

options.consequence: Your child takes it in and keeps asking.

options.text: Deliver a long, anxious lecture
options.consequence: Answering just what was asked keeps it digestible and the door open; an anxious lecture overwhelms and deters.

scenarios.debrief: Answer just the question asked, simply, and let your child come back for more, rather than over-explaining.

scenarios.hook: Your four-year-old points and asks what a body part is called. You want to answer plainly.
scenarios.relearn: Naming body parts as plainly as elbows removes shame and gives a child the words that keep them safe.

yourLine.text: "That's called a penis (or vulva), it's just the proper name, like elbow or knee."
"We don't say that word, it's rude."

scenarios.hook: You want to teach your young child the 'safe grown-up' rule simply. You explain it.
scenarios.relearn: A clear 'tell me, you'll never be in trouble' rule gives a child permission to disclose, unlike 'obey grown-ups'.

yourLine.text: "If anyone touches your private parts or asks you to keep a body secret, tell me, you'll never be in trouble."
"Just be good and do what grown-ups say."

scenarios.hook: Sort: teaches a young child body safety, or accidentally undermines it?
scenarios.relearn: 'You can say no' and 'no body secrets' build safety; 'always let elders' and 'never refuse adults' undermine it.

items.text: 'You can say no to unwanted touch'
'Always let elders hug and kiss you'
'Tell me anything, no secrets about bodies'

scenarios.hook: Match each young-child question to a simple, honest answer.
scenarios.relearn: Young children's body questions each have a simple, honest, shame-free answer that keeps them curious and safe.

pairs.left: 'Why is my body different from my sibling's?'
pairs.right: Bodies come in different kinds, both are normal
A calm, correct, one-line answer

pairs.left: 'Can I say no to a hug?'
pairs.right: Yes, your body is yours

scenarios.hook: Your pre-teen seems embarrassed about body changes. You want to normalise it warmly.
scenarios.relearn: Warmly normalising the changes and inviting questions replaces embarrassment with reassurance.

yourLine.text: "Everything that's happening to your body is normal and healthy, and you can ask me anything, anytime."
"You're too sensitive about all this."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy pre-teen online habit to encourage, or a risk to address?
scenarios.relearn: Telling you about off things and keeping privacy are healthy; sharing info with or meeting strangers are risks to address.

items.text: Telling you about anything that feels off

scenarios.hook: Your pre-teen asks a frank question about sex, earlier than you expected.
scenarios.relearn: Answer frank pre-teen questions honestly and without shame; being scandalised just sends them elsewhere.

options.text: Answer honestly and age-appropriately, without shame
options.consequence: You keep trust and give safe, true info.

options.text: Act scandalised and refuse to answer
options.consequence: An honest, age-right answer keeps trust and safety; acting scandalised teaches them not to ask you again.

scenarios.debrief: Answer an earlier-than-expected frank question honestly and age-appropriately, without shame.

scenarios.hook: Spot what best prepares a pre-teen for the years ahead.
scenarios.relearn: Prepare a pre-teen with honest prep and an open door, not by leaving them to peers and the feed.

scene.text: Honest prep before changes and online life
Leaving them to learn from peers and feeds
An open door for any worry

scenarios.why: Honest prep and an open door prepare a pre-teen; leaving them to peers and feeds leaves them exposed.

scenarios.hook: Your teen asks about something explicit they saw online. You want to stay unflustered.
scenarios.relearn: Meeting an explicit question with calm porn-literacy keeps you the trusted source over the algorithm.

yourLine.text: "Thanks for asking me, a lot of that isn't how real life or real respect works, let's talk about what is."
"That's disgusting, I don't want to hear another word."

scenarios.hook: Your teen is being pressured by a partner and confides in you. You want to support, not control.
scenarios.relearn: Supporting their agency while offering help keeps a pressured teen talking to you, unlike taking over.

yourLine.text: "I'm really glad you told me, no one should pressure you, what do you want to do, and how can I help?"
"That's it, you're not seeing them again, end of discussion."

scenarios.hook: Sort: keeps a teen coming to you, or pushes them to hide things?
scenarios.relearn: Calm listening and respecting autonomy keep a teen coming to you; punishing honesty and snooping make them hide.

scenarios.hook: Your teen makes a choice about relationships you disagree with.
scenarios.relearn: Keep the door open on choices you dislike; ultimatums cost you both influence and trust.

options.text: Stay connected and share your view while keeping the door open
options.consequence: You keep influence and their trust.

options.text: Issue ultimatums that end the conversation
options.consequence: Staying connected keeps both your influence and their trust; ultimatums end the conversation and your sway with it.

scenarios.debrief: Stay connected and share your view on a teen's choice while keeping the door open, rather than issuing ultimatums.

scenarios.hook: Your child asks something where your values are strong. You want to give facts and your view honestly.
scenarios.relearn: Pairing the honest facts with your stated values gives a child both safety and your guidance to weigh.

yourLine.text: "Here's how it actually works, and here's what we believe about it in our family, both matter."
"Never mind the facts, just do as we say."

scenarios.hook: Sort: an honest fact a child needs for safety, or a value you choose to share?
scenarios.relearn: How bodies and consent work are safety facts; the 'right time' and your hopes are values you choose to share.

items.text: When your family feels is the right time
Consent and how to stay safe

scenarios.hook: Sort: protects a child, or leaves them exposed?
scenarios.relearn: Honest facts with values and an open door protect; silence and ceding to the feed leave a child exposed.

scenarios.hook: You worry that giving facts will clash with what grandparents want kept quiet.
scenarios.relearn: Prioritise your child's safety facts over keeping the silence elders prefer; do it kindly, but do it.

options.text: Give your child the safety facts while respecting elders kindly
options.consequence: Your child stays informed and safe.

options.text: Withhold facts to keep the peace at home
options.consequence: Giving safety facts kindly keeps your child informed; withholding them for peace leaves your child unsafe.

scenarios.debrief: Give your child the safety facts they need while handling elders kindly; don't withhold them to keep the peace.

scenarios.hook: Match a values-laden question to a both-and reply.
scenarios.relearn: Values-laden questions each get a both-and reply: honest facts first, then your family's view.

pairs.right: Here are the facts; here's what we believe
Let's separate facts from pressure, and our values
The honest reasons, plus our family's view

scenarios.hook: You froze on a question yesterday and want to go back and repair it. You reopen it.
scenarios.relearn: Going back to repair a fumbled answer models honesty and shows your child the door is genuinely always open.

yourLine.text: "I didn't answer you well yesterday, I was caught off guard, let's talk about it properly now."
"Let's just forget you ever asked that."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a realistic, sustainable parenting-talk habit, or an unrealistic one?
scenarios.relearn: Tiny everyday talks and answering as questions arise are realistic; a formal lecture or waiting to feel expert aren't.

items.text: Tiny talks in the car or at bedtime
Waiting until you feel fully expert

scenarios.hook: Spot the move that makes a parent more askable over time.
scenarios.relearn: Become more askable by welcoming questions and repairing missteps, not by reacting with anger or panic.

scene.text: Welcoming questions without shame
Reacting with anger or panic
Repairing when you get one wrong

scenarios.why: Welcoming questions and repairing mistakes make you more askable; anger and panic make you less.

scenarios.relearn: Each age has a headline focus: body safety young, puberty prep before, and consent and relationships in the teens.
